tabs.title: Installations
tabs.story: Our journey starts in an empty folder. Before any 3D appears, we set up a tiny workshop: two files and one script tag that brings Babylon.js in from a CDN.

sections.p: Don’t want to set anything up? The Babylon.js Playground runs and shares snippets right in the browser. For a real project, follow the steps below.
Make a folder with two files: `index.html` for the page and `main.js` for your code. No installs and no build tools.
sections.code:
mkdir my-babylon-app
cd my-babylon-app
touch index.html main.js
sections.tip: You can also just create both files in your code editor.

sections.p: A CDN is a fast public server that hosts the library. One script tag downloads Babylon.js and creates a global object named `BABYLON`, so every class starts with `BABYLON.` and no `import` is needed.
sections.cap: Your page loads the CDN script, then your own script
sections.code:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang='en'>
<head>
  <meta charset='UTF-8'>
  <meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0'>
  <title>Babylon.js Tutorial</title>
</head>
<body>
  <script src='https://cdn.babylonjs.com/babylon.js'></script>
  <script src='main.js'></script>
</body>
</html>
sections.tip: Load Babylon.js first and your own script second. `main.js` needs `BABYLON` to exist already.

sections.p: Put this line in `main.js`, open `index.html` in your browser and look at the console.
sections.code: console.log(BABYLON.Engine.Version); // prints the Babylon.js version

sections.p: Opening the file directly works for now. Later, loading images, fonts, models and sounds needs a local server, because browsers block those requests on `file://` pages. Any one of these is enough; then open `http://localhost:8000`.
sections.code:
# Python
python3 -m http.server 8000

# or Node
npx serve .

# or use the Live Server extension in VS Code
sections.tip: Live Server also reloads the page every time you save.

tabs.title: The 4 Horsemen
tabs.story: Every Babylon.js app, however big, rides on the same four things. We meet them one by one and end with a working first scene.

sections.p: The `<canvas>` is the space on your page. The Engine is the brain that turns your logic into 3D graphics. The Scene is the 3D space. The Camera shows one area of that space.
sections.cap: The four building blocks of every app

sections.p: Place it before the script tags.
sections.code:
<body>
  <canvas id='renderCanvas'></canvas>
  <script src='https://cdn.babylonjs.com/babylon.js'></script>
  <script src='main.js'></script>
</body>

sections.p: In `main.js`, grab the canvas and give it to the engine so it knows where to draw. There is no `import`: the CDN script already made `BABYLON` available.
sections.code:
const canvas = document.getElementById('renderCanvas');
const engine = new BABYLON.Engine(canvas);

sections.p: Put all your app logic in a `createScene` function that returns a scene. Calling `render()` draws one frame.
Animation, in a video or a game, is a sequence of pictures called frames. One `render()` call gives a still image. A render loop calls it many times per second, as fast as the device allows.
sections.cap: Many frames per second make motion
sections.tip: Congratulations: your first app is running! The console warns that the camera is missing, so we fix that next.

sections.p: Babylon.js can make a default camera and light for you. We study real cameras later. Add this inside `createScene()`.
sections.code: scene.createDefaultCameraOrLight(true, false, true);

sections.p: A little CSS in the `<head>` makes the canvas fill the page.
Resize the window and a cube would stretch. Tell the engine each time the window changes size.
Make `main.js` look like this. Every later tab adds code where it says `the fun stuff`.

tabs.title: MeshBuilder
tabs.story: The stage is ready but empty. MeshBuilder is the workshop that fills it. Every call has the same shape: a name, an options object and the scene.

sections.p: Any object in a scene is a mesh: a simple box, a torus knot, or a complex model from Blender. `MeshBuilder` is a helper class that builds common ones in one line. We build five; explore the others as homework.
sections.cap: Three of the shapes we build

sections.p: The name helps you find the mesh later (we use it for picking). Raise `segments` for a smoother ball, and use `diameterY` to stretch one axis.
sections.cap: More segments means more triangles and more detail

sections.p: Use `size` for a cube, or `width`, `height` and `depth` one by one. `faceColors` paints each face. A Color4 has red, green, blue and opacity; Color3 skips opacity.
sections.tip: The scene argument is optional when your app has only one scene.

sections.p: A flat rectangle with a width and height. `subdivisions` cuts it into a grid, like a sphere’s segments. You can’t see the grid until you switch on wireframe. Use `subdivisionsX` and `subdivisionsY` for different counts.
sections.cap: Subdivisions matter when you move vertices to shape terrain

sections.p: A height map is a grayscale image: the whiter a pixel, the higher the point; the blacker, the lower. Put the image in `images/` and pass its path.
sections.cap: Brightness in the image turns into height
sections.tip: Default subdivisions is 1, so raise it to see detail, but more subdivisions cost more performance. `minHeight` and `maxHeight` set the altitude range.

sections.p: 3D text needs a font in JSON format (convert a `.ttf` with a tool like Facetype.js and put it in a `fonts` folder) plus the `earcut` library, which cuts letter shapes into triangles. Add its CDN script to `index.html`, before `main.js`.
sections.code:
<script src='https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/earcut/2.2.4/earcut.min.js'></script>
<script src='https://cdn.babylonjs.com/babylon.js'></script>
<script src='main.js'></script>

sections.p: Loading the font is asynchronous, so `createScene` becomes `async` and the render loop starts once the scene is ready. The arguments are: name, text, font data, options and scene. Babylon.js finds the global `earcut` by itself.
sections.tip: Use your own converted font file name instead of `GreatVibes.json`.

tabs.title: Cameras
tabs.story: Shapes are on stage, so now we choose how the audience looks. Babylon.js has many cameras, but most apps use only two.

sections.p: Think first-person shooter: the mouse picks the direction and the arrow keys move. It takes a name, a start position and the scene. First remove the default camera and add a default light.
sections.cap: Walk around, or orbit a target

sections.p: It orbits a target. Its constructor takes a name, alpha, beta, radius, target and scene. `setPosition` lets you place it with plain coordinates instead of angles.
Beta limits vertical rotation, alpha limits horizontal rotation, and radius limits how near or far the camera can be.

tabs.title: Materials
tabs.story: Our shapes are bare. A mesh is made of points and lines that give it shape, plus a material that covers them. Colors and textures live in the material.

sections.p: Create a `StandardMaterial` and assign it. Nothing changes yet, but now we can restyle the sphere.
`diffuseColor` is the main color. `specularColor` colors the highlight spot made by a light. Both depend on a light; with no light you get a dark object.
sections.code:
sphereMaterial.diffuseColor = new BABYLON.Color3(0.9, 0.2, 0.4);
sphereMaterial.specularColor = new BABYLON.Color3(0, 1, 0);

sections.p: `ambientColor` only works if the scene’s `ambientColor` has non-zero values in the same channels. `emissiveColor` colors the mesh even without light. `alpha` sets opacity. `wireframe` shows the mesh’s skeleton.
Set `diffuseTexture` for a picture that needs light. Use `emissiveTexture` if the picture should show without any light.
sections.tip: Put your own image in `images/`, and use your file name.

sections.h: A different picture on each face
sections.p: Cut one long image into six blocks. Each block is a Vector4 holding its lower-left and upper-right corners. Add `wrap: true` or the pieces appear flipped.
sections.cap: faceUV maps image blocks to box faces

sections.p: `uOffset` and `vOffset` slide the texture sideways or up and down. `uScale` and `vScale` shrink it to fit the mesh, or repeat it when above 1.
sections.code:
const tex = groundMaterial.emissiveTexture;

tex.uOffset = 1.4;  // move left or right
tex.vOffset = 1.4;  // move up or down

tex.uScale = 3;     // repeat 3 times across
tex.vScale = 2;     // repeat 2 times along

tabs.title: Transformations and Gizmos
tabs.story: New meshes appear at (0, 0, 0). To place them, we move, turn and stretch them, and then use gizmos to do the same with our mouse.

sections.p: Every mesh has `position`, `rotation` (in radians) and `scaling`. Change one axis at a time, or assign a whole Vector3.
sections.cap: The three axes and the three dials

sections.p: Gizmos are handy for debugging, and you can even ship them. Create a `UtilityLayerRenderer` (recommended) and attach the gizmo to a mesh.
Rotating and scaling work the same way. A `PlaneRotationGizmo` turns the mesh around just one axis, so it needs that axis and a color.
sections.tip: Try one gizmo at a time to keep the scene readable.

tabs.title: Animation
tabs.story: Back to the render loop. A 3D scene is a flipbook of frames, so animating just means changing something a little on every frame. We go from easiest to most flexible.

sections.p: The easiest way. Your function runs before every frame. This one turns the box by 0.01 radians about 60 times per second.

One call. Arguments: name, mesh, property, frames per second, total frames, start value, end value. Here 120 frames at 30 fps is 4 seconds. By default it loops forever; the last two arguments are optional (play once, and an easing).
sections.code:
BABYLON.Animation.CreateAndStartAnimation(
  'xScaleAnimation', box, 'scaling.x',
  30,    // frames per second
  120,   // total frames
  0, 2,  // from, to
  BABYLON.Animation.ANIMATIONLOOPMODE_CONSTANT, // play once
  new BABYLON.CircleEase()                       // easing
);

sections.p: The most control. Make an Animation, give it keyframes (a frame number plus a value), attach it to the mesh, then begin. Want it slower? Use a bigger last frame number.
sections.cap: Keyframes are the dots; Babylon.js fills in between

tabs.title: Lights
tabs.story: A scene without light is a dark room. Good lighting changes everything, and Babylon.js offers four types. For these experiments, use a clean scene with an ArcRotateCamera and a ground, and no default light.

sections.p: Point lights shine in every direction, spotlights in a cone, directional lights send parallel rays, and hemispheric lights give soft ambient light.
It shines in all directions, like a candle. It takes a name, a position and the scene. A `LightGizmo` shows where the light is.
A cone of light, like theatre lighting. Arguments: name, position, direction, cone angle, decay with distance, scene. `range` is the farthest it reaches.
Parallel rays from one direction, like the sun far away. It needs only a name, a direction and the scene.
Soft light from sky and ground. The direction points to the sky. `groundColor` lights the opposite side, `diffuse` is the main color and `specular` colors the highlights.

tabs.title: Shadow
tabs.story: You can’t talk about light without shadows. A shadow needs three actors: one that casts it, one that receives it, and a light.

sections.p: Use a ground as the receiver, a named sphere as the caster, and a directional light.
sections.cap: Light, caster, receiver: all three are needed

sections.p: Each shadow-casting light needs one. The first argument is the shadow quality (low values look pixelated), the second is the light. Then list casters and receivers.
`setDarkness` controls the shadow strength (0 is fully dark, 1 means no shadow). The exponential blur map removes pixelated edges, and kernel blur gives the soft edges real shadows have.

tabs.title: Fog
tabs.story: Fog adds atmosphere and hides the far distance. Babylon.js has four fog modes: none, linear, exponential and exponential squared.

sections.p: Density grows steadily with distance from the camera. `fogStart` is where fog begins and `fogEnd` is where objects vanish completely.
sections.cap: The farther away, the thicker the fog

sections.p: EXP and EXP2 thicken faster with distance (EXP2 faster still). They use a density instead of a start and end.
sections.code:
scene.fogMode = BABYLON.Scene.FOGMODE_EXP;   // or FOGMODE_EXP2
scene.fogDensity = 0.2;

sections.p: Match the fog to your background and distant objects melt away.
sections.code: scene.fogColor = new BABYLON.Color3(0.3, 0.2, 0.6);

tabs.title: Picking Objects (Raycast)
tabs.story: Now we make the world interactive. When you click, Babylon.js shoots an invisible ray from the pointer into the scene and tells you what it hit.

sections.p: A pointer event can be a mouse move, a click or a screen touch. `onPointerDown` fires on press, and `scene.pick` returns whatever is under the pointer.
sections.cap: A click becomes a ray that returns the mesh it hits

sections.p: The hit could be the ground, the sphere, or nothing at all. First check that a mesh was picked, then check its name. This is why we named our meshes.
sections.tip: Skip the `pickedMesh` check and clicking empty space throws an error.

tabs.title: Loading and Animating Models
tabs.story: Real projects rarely build everything from primitives. They load models made in Blender or downloaded from the web, often with ready-made animations.

sections.p: The `.babylon` format works out of the box. For `.gltf`, `.glb` or `.obj` you also load the loaders script from the CDN, after Babylon.js and before `main.js`.
sections.cap: A model file goes through a loader into your scene
sections.code:
<script src='https://cdn.babylonjs.com/babylon.js'></script>
<script src='https://cdn.babylonjs.com/loaders/babylonjs.loaders.min.js'></script>
<script src='main.js'></script>

sections.p: Put the file in `models/`. Arguments: which meshes to load (`null` for all), the folder, the file name, the scene, and an optional callback that runs when loading finishes.
Models can carry several animation groups. The first one plays by default, so stop it and play another. Passing `true` makes it loop.
sections.tip: Index 5 belongs to the fox model. Log `animationGroups` to see which animations your model has.

sections.p: The promise-based version. Both methods are asynchronous.

tabs.title: Sound
tabs.story: A world feels empty without a soundtrack. Adding ambient music takes a single object.

sections.p: Put your audio file in `audio/`. A `Sound` takes a name, the file path, the scene, a callback for when loading ends, and an options object.
sections.cap: Load a file, then loop it in the background
sections.tip: Browsers often block sound until the visitor interacts with the page.

sections.p: Skip `autoplay` and start or stop the sound from your own code, for example on a click.

tabs.title: Tools
tabs.story: One thing that sets Babylon.js apart is its tool set. These tools make debugging easier and let you share work with the community.

sections.p: The Playground (used all through the original tutorial) writes and shares snippets online. The Inspector, Sandbox and Node Material Editor cover debugging, previewing and shaders.
sections.cap: Debug, preview, and build shaders without code

sections.p: A visual panel to explore and edit your scene live: objects, textures, materials and animations. You can take screenshots, record video, and export the scene as `.babylon` or `.gltf`.
Drop a model into the Sandbox to preview and inspect it before you use it in a project.
Build shaders by connecting nodes, with no code at all. Shaders are an advanced topic for another day.
sections.tip: A shader is a small program that tells the graphics card how to color each pixel.

tabs.title: Final Thoughts
tabs.story: We started in an empty folder and now have shapes, cameras, materials, motion, lights, shadows, fog, clicks, models and sound.

sections.p: This is only the surface of what Babylon.js can do, so keep experimenting. A good first project: a room with a textured floor, a spotlight and a rotating box that changes color when clicked. Then load a model and add background music.

This guide follows the storyline of ‘Babylon.js Tutorial for Absolute Beginners’ by Wael Yasmina, retold with new graphics, short code samples and plain CDN script tags instead of npm. The original used an Earth heightmap, the Great Vibes font, a SPY-HYPERSPORT texture and a Fox model.
